train_config.objective: same as shipped actor_disc.pt: CE(fmove sign class) + CE(smove sign class) + 10*MSE(tanh(yaw)) + BCEWithLogits(jump), Adam
train_config.data: pipeline/out/policy/{S,A,SP}.npy, train split only (SP==0), same build() as the shipped policy

parity.source: S.npy[SP==2] (held-out test split, never seen by train_disc)

loss_curve_diagnosis.loss_curve_shape: flat and noisy from the first logged point (20k steps) through 120k: 0.9953, 1.0482, 0.9701, 0.9721, 0.9457, 0.9517 -- no visible descent, does not distinguish 'converged early' from 'stuck early' by itself.

class_balance_train_split.note: same underlying (S,A) data feeds both the 2x256 and 3x512 runs, so this imbalance is a property of the task/data, not something introduced by training the larger network.

marginal_entropy_floor_nats.interpretation: the two CE terms alone would sum to about 2.0 nats for a model that learned nothing but the class marginals; the actually-observed total loss (which also includes 10*MSE(yaw) and BCE(jump)) sits far below that already at the first logged point (20k steps), so substantial learning happened before logging started -- consistent with fast early convergence followed by a plateau, not with an optimizer that never got moving.

loss_curve_diagnosis.confound_not_ruled_out: train_disc's printed loss is a single random minibatch of 1024 (not a smoothed running average or a fixed eval-set loss), so batch-to-batch sampling variance alone is enough to make a genuinely-still-improving curve look flat/noisy at this scale of improvement. No comparable per-step loss log exists for the original 2x256 run (its train_disc() predates this task's logging change and only printed to stdout, which was not captured), so there is no direct within-setup baseline to confirm the flat shape is shared across both network sizes rather than specific to the larger one.

held_out_generalization_evidence.train_val_test_gap: old net: quadrant agreement 66.9%/67.0%/66.6% (train/val/test); new net: 68.8%/68.4%/68.3%. Both nets show <0.5pp train-vs-held-out gap -- no overfitting artifact in either -- and the new net's improvement over the old one is consistent in sign and similar in size across ALL THREE splits and ALL SEVEN reported metrics.
held_out_generalization_evidence.significance: a training pathology specific to the larger net (bad LR, unstable optimization, dead units) would be expected to show up as *worse* or erratic held-out behaviour, or a widened train/val gap, relative to the smaller net -- neither is observed. This rules out the strong form of reading 2 ('the larger network is not learning'). It does not rule out the weak form ('a training setup tuned for the larger network specifically -- LR schedule, class-weighted CE, more steps -- would realize a bigger gain than the ~1-2pp measured here').

loss_curve_diagnosis.conclusion: Evidence leans toward reading 1 (the task is close to its ceiling for this 14-dim feature set) over the strong form of reading 2, but 'bought nothing' is empirically false: the 3x512 policy beats the 2x256 policy on every one of the 7 reported held-out metrics, on both val and test, by consistent (if modest: ~1-2 percentage points on the classification metrics, several units on MAE) margins, with no sign of overfitting in either network. The flat/noisy composite loss curve does not by itself prove either reading: it is a single noisy minibatch quantity, not a smoothed or fixed-eval-set metric, and the marginal-entropy calculation above shows the model was already well past the 'predict-only-the-class-frequencies' floor by the first logged point (20k steps), so a fast-early/flat-later shape is exactly what a well-behaved run would look like too.
what_i_would_change_if_rerunning_to_test: log loss on a fixed, held-out eval batch (a few thousand rows, same batch every log step) instead of a fresh random training minibatch, to get a low-noise curve that can actually distinguish 'still improving slowly' from 'genuinely flat'

add class-weighted CrossEntropyLoss (or focal loss) for the f/s heads given the measured 8.8%/46%/45% and 28%/44%/28% imbalance -- this affects both network sizes equally today, so removing it as a confound would clarify whether the extra capacity is being spent on the rare class or wasted

add an LR schedule (warmup + decay, or just a lower flat LR) for the 512-wide network -- wider layers typically want a smaller per-parameter step size at fixed batch size, and a flat 3e-4 for the whole run could be too coarse to let the last stretch of optimization resolve into a visible descent rather than noise

train for materially more steps (or a larger batch) at the same LR, since 537k params over 120k steps at batch 1024 gives the wider network fewer effective gradient updates per parameter than the 71.7k-param network had at the same step count
log gradient norms per layer (especially the third hidden layer, the one depth=3 adds over the shipped network) to check directly whether it is contributing signal or sitting near-dead
loss_curve_diagnosis.not_done: none of the above changes were applied -- the instruction was to run the comparison as specified and report the reading, not to tune the result.
